description: I'm competing in this challenge as a solo team. I'm an ambitious high school junior motivated to develop my skills and learn more about space through NASA's Space Apps Challenge. I have participated in previous hackathons and have extensive software experience. By prioritizing knowledge and depth, I carry out successful projects that offer complexity but also ease of use. I hope to do the best I can and expand my understanding of using space data in our projects through this challenge.
summary:
How does a lunar mission get impacted when it is delayed by three days? Astraknot, a Lunar Landing Site Navigator, shows how an arrival delay changes sunlight availability and opportunities for direct-to-Earth communication as the Sun and Earth move relative to surrounding ridges.

Using NASA JPL Horizons and lunar terrain data, the app shows when ridges block the Sun or Earth, helping users assess solar-power potential and direct-to-Earth communication windows simultaneously. Users can watch horizon crossings in 3D, compare up to four locations, highlight steep terrain, and search arrival dates against selected requirements.

The public app includes four documented locations and a precomputed custom-coordinate demonstration. In its guided Odysseus example, a three-day delay reduces the Sun's center's time above the terrain skyline from 90.2% to 72.0% over a 14-day mission.

The project connects accessible visualization with traceable calculations and explicit uncertainty. It assesses geometric visibility for solar power potential and communication windows. It does not calculate electrical power output, guarantee radio-link performance, or determine landing safety.
details:
ASTRAKNOT - Lunar Landing Site Navigator

Github link: https://github.com/dylanisyess/astraknot

Problem: What happens when a lunar landing gets delayed?

A lunar landing location cannot be evaluated independently of time. Surrounding ridges affect when sunlight reaches the surface and when Earth is visible for direct communication. A small arrival delay can cause mass differences in Earth and Sun visibility, affecting the mission's ability to communicate with Earth and harvest solar power.

Lunar Landing Site Navigator visualizes how time differences change a mission in an interactive browser app. Using NASA position and terrain data, it lets users watch the Sun and Earth cross a local skyline, compare locations, test arrival delays, screen steep terrain, and search for arrival windows that meet selected requirements.

Astraknot solves the problem of complicated reconciliation when choosing a landing site based on time constraints.

A mission story users can investigate

The guided example begins at the IM-1 Odysseus landing location with a hypothetical 14-day mission arriving on December 18, 2026. It uses the historical location for a future planning scenario; it does not recreate the actual mission.

In Horizon view, users watch the Sun emerge above a ridge approximately 5.28° high. A smooth-horizon model already considers the Sun visible before it clears that ridge. Over the mission window, the smooth model reports 98.6% sunlight availability, while the terrain model reports 90.2%.

Moving arrival three days later reduces terrain-modeled sunlight availability to 72.0%.

Users can then add Athena through the site comparison control. For the same baseline and delayed windows, Athena’s sunlight availability falls from 86.1% to 64.7%, while Earth visibility falls from 95.0% to 73.6%.

This example connects a visible event—the Sun clearing a ridge—to a mission-level consequence. It also shows why the same delay can affect different locations differently.

Explore: see the geometry behind the numbers

Site overview shows the surrounding terrain, modeled observer, and directions toward the Sun and Earth. Users can orbit the scene and inspect terrain while keeping the observer’s location fixed.

Horizon view places the camera at the modeled observer. Continuous Sun and Earth tracking lets users follow either body as time advances. Crossing controls jump between estimated rises and sets, making it easier to find events within a long dataset.

The timeline distinguishes four conditions: Sun and Earth available together, Sun only, Earth only, and neither. Unknown or missing data has a separate state. A blocked body remains distinguishable from one that is simply outside the camera’s field of view.

Checking conditions at a potential landing site

The Conditions panel brings together three checks that help users judge whether a location fits their mission’s needs. It compares the Sun’s position with the local skyline to assess direct sunlight availability, performs the same comparison for Earth to identify direct-to-Earth communication windows, and checks DEM-derived slopes against the selected threshold to flag steep terrain within 500 metres. It also shows whether sunlight and Earth visibility are available simultaneously and when the next modeled visibility change occurs.

These checks connect the terrain view to practical planning questions: Is sunlight available? Is Earth above the horizon? Is nearby terrain unusually steep? Users can then examine how those conditions change throughout the mission. Favorable results support further investigation; they do not by themselves establish landing safety or guarantee sufficient power and communications performance.

Analysis: compare availability, interruptions, and arrival delays

Analysis turns the scene into a quantitative comparison. Users can compare up to four sites using the same mission dates, duration, and horizon model.

For each site, it reports:

  • The percentage of the mission with direct sunlight.
  • The percentage with Earth above the modeled horizon.
  • The percentage with both available simultaneously.
  • The longest uninterrupted period without direct sunlight.
  • The longest uninterrupted period without Earth visibility.

The distinction between percentages and interruptions matters. Two locations could have similar total sunlight availability but very different lengths of continuous darkness. Those differences are relevant to power-system studies, even though the app itself does not model batteries.

Time plots show how Sun and Earth elevations relate to the modeled horizon. The panorama shows the skyline around the observer, helping explain which terrain directions cause obstructions. Baseline and delayed mission results reveal how shifting arrival by one, three, or seven days changes the comparison.

Analysis also includes terrain statistics for a matched 500-metre radius around each observer. Users can compare steepness alongside visibility without combining them into an arbitrary overall “best site” score.

Outages that touch a mission boundary receive warnings: the reported duration covers the selected window, and the actual interruption may extend beyond it.

Arrival Window Finder: search against explicit requirements

Instead of manually testing dates, users can search daily candidate arrivals at a selected UTC hour. Each candidate must accommodate the complete mission duration within the dataset.

Five ranking options let users prioritize:

  • Greatest sunlight availability.
  • Greatest Earth visibility.
  • Greatest simultaneous Sun and Earth availability.
  • Shortest maximum period without sunlight.
  • Shortest maximum period without Earth visibility.

Optional screening limits let users specify minimum availability percentages and maximum interruption durations. These limits are off by default. Results that satisfy them are labeled “Meets selected limits,” rather than being declared safe or mission-ready.

The finder never relaxes a requirement to produce an answer. If no candidate qualifies, it reports that outcome. Candidates with unknown data cannot pass screening or receive a normal ranking.

A per-site summary shows the best matching arrival for each searched location. Users can expand a result to preview one, three, and seven day delays before applying it. Searches, filters, and previews leave the current mission unchanged; an explicit apply action updates the scenario.

The finder uses unrounded values for ranking and limits, and CSV exports preserve additional precision. Its results are the best among the searched daily candidates, not a continuous-time optimum.

Scientific problems addressed during development

The local horizon is not necessarily nearby.

A small terrain patch can look convincing while omitting distant ridges that affect visibility. The pipeline therefore calculates terrain directions in Moon-centered three-dimensional geometry, accounting for lunar curvature and checking distant terrain against a conservative elevation bound.

The custom-coordinate demonstration made this especially clear. Terrain more than 50 kilometres away raised parts of its skyline by as much as approximately 2.36°. A local-only terrain patch would have missed those obstructions.

For a selected 14-day window at that point, a smooth horizon reports 71.13% simultaneous Sun and Earth visibility, while the terrain horizon reports 0%. The window was chosen using a documented comparison rule. This is a specific demonstration of terrain sensitivity, not a claim that every location behaves this way.

A convincing 3D surface is not automatically an accurate visibility model.

During development, comparisons between the rendered terrain mesh and calculated skyline found disagreements reaching approximately 0.11° at some sites. Near the horizon, that is enough to make a body appear hidden when the visibility calculation says otherwise.

The solution separates display geometry from the authoritative skyline. Site overview retains the terrain mesh, while Horizon view uses the exported skyline to control occlusion. The app reports the remaining mesh limitation rather than treating visual agreement as proof of scientific accuracy.

Sampling and instantaneous geometry can disagree near a crossing.

The dataset uses 10-minute steps. Each interval’s visibility classification represents its midpoint, while the displayed body position corresponds to the selected time. Near a rise or set, those can fall on opposite sides of the skyline.

The app preserves both values and explains the situation with a near-crossing message. It does not move the Sun or Earth to force agreement with a label. Crossing times remain estimates on the sampling grid.

Rounded numbers can hide meaningful interruptions.

A mission with a brief sunlight interruption can round to “100.0%” availability. That presentation would obscure exactly the kind of event the app is meant to expose.

The interface reserves exact 100% and 0% displays for exact values. Near those endpoints, it uses bounded labels such as “>99.9%,” and short interruptions appear in minutes. Screening and ranking always use the underlying values.

Terrain screening at a stated measurement scale

The app calculates slopes from source elevation data, independently of the simplified rendering mesh. Steep-terrain highlighting, a full slope map, and point inspection show where slopes exceed a selected threshold.

The default 15° threshold is illustrative and adjustable. The analysis covers a 500-metre radius around each observer, with missing data distinguished from flat ground.

Source resolution matters: approximately 20-metre terrain cells at the polar sites measure slope across roughly 40 metres, while Apollo 17’s approximately 60-metre cells measure it across roughly 120 metres. These products describe broader steepness, not individual boulders, fine roughness, or bearing strength.

Inspecting a terrain point does not move the modeled observer or silently recalculate mission visibility for a different location.

NASA data and the preparation pipeline

NASA JPL Horizons supplies apparent Sun and Earth directions from each modeled observer. Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA products supply polar elevations, with broader terrain products supporting distant skyline calculations. Apollo 17 uses SLDEM2015, which combines LOLA measurements with terrain information from JAXA’s SELENE/Kaguya mission.

The pipeline calculates a skyline in 3,600 directions around each observer. The expanded release covers December 1, 2026, through March 31, 2027, with 10-minute sampling and an observer approximately one metre above the modeled surface.

Preparation runs ahead of time. The public app serves cached results without requiring live NASA requests, an AI model, or a processing server during normal use.

Custom coordinates and current coverage

The public catalog includes Athena, Odysseus, Apollo 17, Connecting Ridge CR1, and a prepared custom-coordinate demonstration at 85.5° S, 315.0° E. Labels distinguish historical landing locations, a notional study point, and a user-defined coordinate.

The reusable pipeline can prepare additional coordinates where the required terrain coverage is available. Support is established through coverage and validation checks; a coordinate is not accepted solely because it falls within a broad geographic region.

The public website currently offers the completed demonstration point, not on-demand processing of arbitrary coordinates. Public processing would require additional hosting, queue management, and verification.

Verification and limits

The project includes automated tests for calculations, interval boundaries, missing data, search behavior, and interface interactions. The final interface review passed 439 frontend tests, type checking, and a production build. Dataset validation and regression checks protect existing scientific outputs when features change.

The app supports education and early mission studies. It assesses geometric sunlight availability and direct-to-Earth visibility windows; it does not calculate electrical power output, battery endurance, antenna performance, or a complete communications link budget.

Visibility uses body centers rather than a partial-disk illumination model. Terrain resolution, coordinate assumptions, and sampling affect the results. CR1 remains provisional, and the documented Odysseus elevation discrepancy remains unresolved. Terrain screening is not a landing-safety certification.

What the project contributes

Lunar Landing Site Navigator makes the connection between terrain and timing inspectable. Users can see an obstruction, understand its effect on a mission window, compare another location, and search for alternatives using the same underlying calculations. Its value is in connecting the terrain geometry and consequences, allowing users to test decisions more easily.

Use of AI tools

ChatGPT, OpenAI Codex, and Anthropic Claude through Claude Code assisted with brainstorming, research, coding, debugging, test development, interface design, and writing. Project decisions and outputs were reviewed through automated tests, data checks, and hands-on application testing.

The demonstration video uses CapCut text-to-speech narration and an AI-generated closing title card, with visible disclosure. OBS Studio recorded the working application.

NASA source measurements and ephemerides were not generated by AI. The app calculates its results deterministically from those sources and does not use an AI model during normal operation.
